content: A left shift, also known as a blood shift, refers to an increase in the number of immature leukocytes, particularly neutrophil band cells, in the peripheral blood. In less common cases, the term may also describe a similar phenomenon in severe erythroanemia, where reticulocytes and immature erythrocyte precursors are observed in the peripheral circulation. The standard definition of a left shift is an absolute band form count exceeding 700 cells per microliter. The term originates from historical laboratory practices, where band form counts were recorded on the far left side of paper laboratory reports. Morphologically, a left shift is typically identified during microscopic examination of a blood smear. This systemic response to inflammation is most frequently observed in the context of active infections and other severe illnesses, such as hypoxia and shock. In cases of sepsis or severe inflammatory responses, Döhle bodies may also be present in the cytoplasm of neutrophils. The pathogenesis of a left shift is thought to involve cytokines, including interleukin-1 (IL-1) and tumor necrosis factor (TNF), which accelerate the release of cells from the postmitotic reserve pool in the bone marrow. This process results in an increased number of immature cells in the peripheral blood.
